demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: Arjun sits across from me, fingers tracing the rim of his coffee cup. He is thirty-nine, a man who has spent the last decade mapping open-concept living rooms and sourcing stone countertops for other people’s homes. Today, his own space feels suffocating. The rupture happens in late autumn, on a Tuesday evening, when his brother, Karim, collapses in a grocery store parking lot. A silent cardiac event. No warning. Just the sudden, absolute stop of a life Arjun had planned to share with for another forty years. At first, he moves through his house like a ghost in his own blueprint. He stops sleeping past two a.m. When he drifts off, the carpeted aisle of the grocery store materializes behind his eyelids, accompanied by the smell of spilled coffee and the frantic, useless shouts of strangers. He wakes with his heart hammering against his ribs, certain for a few breathless seconds that he stands there, pressing down on a chest that refuses to rise. By the third week, he cancels all client meetings. The idea of walking through a newly tiled bathroom, of discussing the weight of a chandelier, feels obscene. The world continues to demand color palettes and floor plans, but Arjun’s mind refuses to hold any image that isn’t fractured. He starts wearing noise-canceling headphones while driving. He avoids the news. He avoids the phone. He tells his wife, Priya, that he is “just resting,” but his eyes stay fixed on the hallway mirror, watching for a reflection that suddenly isn’t there. Now, months later, the avoidance hardens into a quiet architecture of isolation. At the office, his assistant handles the site visits. Arjun stays at his desk, sketching the same corner of a room over and over until the lines blur. He knows he should be pushing through, that the firm expects deliveries, but the pressure in his chest when his phone vibrates feels like a physical weight. He checks his voicemail with dread, half-expecting another hospital call. When Priya tries to hug him, his body tenses before he can stop it. He lets her hold him, but his mind drifts elsewhere, cataloging the exits in the room, counting the floorboards beneath his feet, calculating how many seconds it would take to reach the front door if something goes wrong. He catches himself scanning crowded restaurants for people who look like him, not for comfort, but because his nervous system has learned to treat familiarity as a threat. The work focuses on creating harmony, but now every layout feels like a trap. He refuses to approve any project with long corridors or narrow doorways, telling himself it’s about “sightlines,” yet his assistant notices he leaves by five thirty. The guilt sits heavy in his stomach, a constant companion. He replays the parking lot scene during every quiet moment, wondering if he had said the right thing, if he had noticed the pallor, if he had simply been looking at his phone. The questions loop without resolution. He stops attending Friday prayers, not from a loss of faith, but because the crowded prayer hall triggers a startle response that makes him feel like he breathes through a straw. Priya speaks to him gently, but he feels the distance between them widening like a poorly scaled floor plan. He loves her, but the grief carves a room inside him that he cannot invite her into. He sits in his study each evening, staring at a sample board of walnut veneer, tracing the grain with his thumb, waiting for the panic to subside so he can remember what it feels like to be still.
